strengths: The natural-scene two-dot experiment is a worthwhile extension of classical object-grouping psychophysics: 72 participants, 255 images, four counterbalanced conditions, eye-tracked fixation control, and approximately 1,020 image-condition trials provide a potentially useful behavioral resource.

The paper asks a timely computer-vision question and evaluates a reasonably broad collection of supervised, self-supervised, Transformer, and convolutional representations. The consistent advantage of DINO-family features across grouping accuracy, reaction-time prediction, and mask-recovery AUC is interesting.

The patch-affinity analysis is intuitive and visually interpretable. Layer-wise results and the comparison between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment provide a coherent descriptive account of what may distinguish the stronger models.

The Gram-alignment experiment goes beyond passive model comparison and produces sizable improvements across four supervised models. The manuscript is generally clear, well motivated, and supported by informative figures.
weaknesses: The principal reaction-time result may suffer from serious cross-validation leakage. The 1,020 trials comprise four dot configurations for each of only 255 images, but the stated 10-fold split operates over trials rather than grouping all configurations of an image into the same fold. Consequently, test images—and the identical central-patch feature—can appear in training, allowing a high-capacity MLP to learn image-specific difficulty. Evaluation with image-grouped folds is necessary for the claimed generalization to unseen scenes.

The reaction-time evidence lacks essential controls and uncertainty estimates. There are no baselines using only condition, dot distance, object geometry, mask size, grouping-classifier confidence, or human accuracy; no within-condition evaluation is reported; and Figure 4 provides neither raw correlations nor fold/bootstrap confidence intervals. Thus, reproducing the four condition means does not establish that representations explain fine-grained human perceptual difficulty.

The claimed mechanistic or causal role of Gram structure is not isolated. Gram-aligned models receive additional fine-tuning and privileged supervision from DINOv3, but there is no matched fine-tuning control, alternative or shuffled teacher, feature-distillation baseline, or ablation of the Gram loss. The experiment shows that a particular DINOv3 distillation procedure helps, not that Gram structure itself is the operative mechanism.

The conclusion that training objective matters more than architecture is not supported by a controlled factorial comparison. Models differ in pretraining data, recipes, patch sizes or spatial resolutions, and distillation; notably, DINOv3 ConvNeXt is distilled from a Transformer. These differences also make the nine-point cross-model correlation in Figure 6 non-independent and confounded. Its correlation coefficient, uncertainty, and leave-one-family-out robustness are not reported.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits the Gram loss equation, layer matching and weights, training schedule and classification-retention results; MLP hidden dimensions, regularization, optimization and target preprocessing; reaction-time exclusion or outlier procedures; precise image preprocessing and dot-to-token mapping; and a definition of how per-head features in Figure 5C are obtained. No dataset or code release commitment is stated.

The proposed object-centric metric is essentially central-patch-to-COCO-mask retrieval AUC and does require object annotations for evaluation, contrary to the contribution statement that it operates without object-level supervision. Its novelty relative to established dense-feature and unsupervised segmentation evaluations is limited, and sensitivity to object size, boundary patches, background, patch resolution, and ROC aggregation is not analyzed.

The behavioral study is described mostly through condition averages without inferential statistics or participant-level mixed-effects analysis. Likewise, grouping accuracies have no seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. These omissions make it difficult to determine whether several model differences are reliable.

No contribution type is declared, so I assessed the paper as Algorithms/General. It also has a meaningful Datasets/Benchmarks component, but the absence of a release plan, benchmark protocol robust to image leakage, and detailed documentation prevents that framing from resolving the evidential concerns. Overall, the premise and dataset are promising, but the central behavioral and mechanistic claims are not yet convincingly supported.

The behavioral experiment is a meaningful expansion of the classical two-dot paradigm: 72 participants, eye-tracked fixation control, 255 natural images, four counterbalanced conditions, and 1,020 image-condition trials.
The comparison includes supervised, self-supervised, Transformer, and convolutional models. The consistent advantage of DINO-family features is an interesting empirical observation.

The object-centric AUC provides an intuitive summary of how token affinity corresponds to annotated object regions, and the layer-wise analysis suggests that this structure becomes stronger in deeper DINOv3 layers.
The Gram-alignment intervention is potentially useful: transferring spatial similarity structure improves grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC, and behavioral prediction across four student models.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess the work as Algorithms/General, while recognizing that its strongest element is arguably the behavioral benchmark. Under either framing, the evidence and reproducibility are insufficient: there is no stated release plan for stimuli, trial-level behavioral data, preprocessing code, or trained probes.

The reaction-time evaluation uses random 10-fold cross-validation over the 1,020 trials even though four trials derive from each image. Consequently, variants of the same image can occur in both training and test folds, sharing the central token and much scene content. Image-grouped cross-validation is necessary to establish generalization rather than within-image interpolation.

The behavioral modeling lacks essential controls. There are no predictors based only on condition, dot distance, segmentation geometry, boundary distance, low-level image features, or grouping confidence. Because the dominant human effects are same/different condition and distance, reproducing the four condition means does not establish that a model explains finer trial-level perceptual difficulty.

The statistical reporting is inadequate. Figure 4 provides no exact correlations, fold or seed variability, confidence intervals, model-comparison tests, or permutation baseline. The human analysis likewise reports means and SEM without inferential statistics, RT exclusion/outlier rules, participant-level variability, or mixed-effects analyses. Correct-trial-only RT analysis can also induce selection bias.

The noise-ceiling normalization is insufficiently justified. Dividing model-to-half-subject correlation by the raw split-half correlation is not the standard correction for attenuation and can inflate normalized values; Spearman-Brown correction or a clearly derived ceiling estimator is needed.

The supposedly supervision-free object-centric metric explicitly requires COCO object masks to compute true- and false-positive rates. Moreover, the 30,000-trial grouping probe is a two-layer nonlinear MLP trained using mask-derived same/different labels. These evaluations can measure accessibility of object information, but they do not by themselves show that the tested system performs grouping without object-level supervision.

The claimed relationship between object-centricity and human alignment is based on only nine highly related models, evaluated on the same images and using closely related token-pair signals. It lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, held-out datasets, and controls for model family, training data, scale, or grouping accuracy. The evidence therefore does not support the stated general principle or the conclusion that training objective matters more than architecture.

The Gram-alignment experiment is not reproducible from the manuscript: the loss definition, layer correspondence, feature normalization, coefficient, teacher treatment, optimizer, schedule, data augmentation, training duration, and classification-retention results are omitted. It is also missing controls such as continued classification fine-tuning, direct feature or attention distillation, alternative relational losses, and randomized teachers.

Gram alignment directly distills pairwise spatial relationships from the strongest DINOv3 teacher, so improvements on similarity-based AUC and token-based probes are expected. Without competing distillation controls, the experiment does not isolate Gram structure as the causal mechanism, making the conclusion that it is an active contributor substantially overstated.

The comparisons confound objective with dataset scale, recipe, generation, and teacher knowledge. In particular, DINO, DINOv2, and DINOv3 are not controlled objective-only comparisons, while DINOv3 ConvNeXt is itself distilled from a strong Transformer. A factorial comparison with matched architecture, data, compute, and optimization is needed.

Several methodological details remain ambiguous, including MLP size and regularization, hyperparameter selection, the definition of per-head features in Figure 5C, aggregation of ROC curves across differently sized objects, handling of unannotated COCO objects/background, and whether incomplete annotations bias false-positive rates.

The participant sample is narrow, and the paper provides no limitations or broader-impact discussion concerning demographic generalization, annotation dependence, or the distinction between behavioral predictivity and mechanistic similarity. Overall, the promising dataset and observations are outweighed by leakage risk, weak controls, missing statistical evidence, and overclaimed causal conclusions.

strengths: The manuscript studies an important and relatively underexplored question: whether object-centric structure in self-supervised vision models predicts human perceptual grouping in natural scenes. The combination of psychophysics and representation analysis is relevant to computer vision and potentially impactful.

The behavioral experiment is thoughtfully designed, with 72 participants, 255 natural images, counterbalanced conditions, distance-matched dot placements, eye tracking, and a substantially larger stimulus set than earlier two-dot studies.

The empirical story is coherent across several measurements: DINO-family models perform well on grouping classification and reaction-time prediction, their patch affinities better respect object boundaries, and Gram alignment improves all three reported metrics. Comparisons between ViT and ConvNeXt variants also provide useful evidence that training regime matters beyond architecture alone.

The presentation is clear and visually effective. The affinity maps, layer/head analyses, ROC curves, and intervention plots make the proposed relationship easy to understand. The discussion also appropriately notes that maximizing object-centricity is not necessarily desirable for every visual task. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/af32007810bc48fd9bd17dd37458049a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess the paper as Algorithms/General under the provided default, although much of its value is closer to Datasets/Benchmarks. Under either framing, reproducibility is currently inadequate: there is no code/data release statement, and essential details of the MLPs, optimization, feature extraction, Gram loss, loss weighting, fine-tuning schedule, and model checkpoints are absent.

The reaction-time evaluation appears to randomly divide 1,020 trials into folds even though each of the 255 images contributes four closely related trials. Consequently, training and test folds can contain different conditions from the same image, sharing the central-dot feature and much scene content. This creates image-level leakage and may let the readout learn image-specific difficulty. Cross-validation should hold out entire images, and preferably report uncertainty across image-grouped splits.

The statistical support is too limited for the strength of the claims. The paper reports no numerical model-human correlations, AUC values, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the central correlation in Fig. 6B is not quantified and is based on only nine related model instances. Human effects are presented as means without mixed-effects analyses, RT exclusion criteria, or inferential tests. This makes it difficult to judge robustness.

The Gram-alignment experiment does not establish that Gram structure is a causal mechanism. Models receive additional ImageNet fine-tuning and teacher supervision, but there is no equally trained classification-only control, conventional feature-distillation baseline, alternative teacher, or shuffled/local Gram control. Improvements could therefore reflect extra training or generic knowledge distillation. The claim that Gram structure is an “active contributor” is stronger than the evidence supports, and the assertion that classification performance is maintained is not accompanied by results.

Several comparisons are confounded. DINO generations differ in training data, recipes, patch sizes, and other design choices, while the architecture-versus-objective conclusion is drawn from a sparse, non-factorial collection of checkpoints. Matching architectures in some comparisons is helpful, but it does not justify the broad claim that objective matters more than architecture.

The claimed object-centric metric is said not to require object-level supervision, yet its ROC computation explicitly relies on ground-truth COCO object masks. The definitions of TPR and FPR are also described as proportions of active patches inside or outside an object, rather than the standard rates conditioned on positive and negative pixels; the exact computation needs clarification. Likewise, the meaning of extracting separate “features” from individual attention heads is not specified.

The behavioral benchmark has promise, but the paper does not discuss its planned availability, participant consent beyond IRB approval, licensing, or the representativeness of a single undergraduate sample. Generalization is evaluated only on COCO scenes and object annotations, leaving open whether the result holds for unseen datasets, ambiguous boundaries, non-photographic imagery, or genuinely out-of-distribution objects. Overall, these concerns slightly outweigh the otherwise compelling idea and positive empirical pattern.

strengths: The work is best viewed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than a new-algorithm paper. Its strongest contribution is a carefully designed natural-scene two-dot benchmark: 72 participants, 255 images, four controlled conditions, eye-tracking-based fixation enforcement, counterbalancing, and approximately 18 observations per image-condition trial.

The human experiment is well motivated and produces sensible psychophysical signatures, including high accuracy (90%), negligible response bias, a same-object advantage, and the expected interaction with dot distance.

The comparison spans supervised and self-supervised Transformers and ConvNeXts. Results are internally coherent: DINO-family representations perform well on grouping, predict reaction times comparatively well, and exhibit high within-object patch affinity. Reporting raw correlations, a linear-readout check, condition-specific correlations, and a CLS-distillation baseline adds useful supporting evidence.

The Gram-alignment intervention is promising: improvements across grouping accuracy, object-centric AUC, and behavioral alignment suggest that patch-similarity structure is a useful target for perceptually aligned representation learning. The paper is generally clear and visually communicates the main results effectively.
weaknesses: The central behavioral evaluation appears to use random trial-level cross-validation over 1,020 trials derived from only 255 images. Because all four conditions for an image share the same scene and central patch, variants of the same image can enter both training and test folds. This is substantial image leakage: the readout may learn scene-specific difficulty or features rather than generalize to unseen scenes. Grouped cross-validation holding out all four trials of each image is essential, and its outcome could materially change the main model ranking and correlations.

The claim that training objective contributes more than architecture is not causally supported by the model set. DINO generations differ in training data, scale, augmentations, and other recipe details; the DINOv3 ConvNeXt is distilled from a Transformer and is therefore not a clean architecture-by-objective control. Factorial comparisons with matched data, capacity, and training budgets are needed.

The Gram experiment does not convincingly isolate Gram structure as the mechanism. Matching a DINOv3 teacher's complete pairwise patch-similarity matrix directly transfers its object-centric information. CLS-token distillation is a weak control because it imposes a fundamentally different, global constraint and is reported only for the ViTs. Necessary controls include identical fine-tuning without Gram loss on all reported metrics, token/feature distillation, shuffled or spatially controlled Gram targets, and alternative teachers. Accordingly, the causal language that Gram structure 'drives' alignment is too strong.

The reported correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment is based on only nine highly dependent, selectively related models. A Spearman correlation of 0.95 and nominal p=0.0001 overstates the evidence because models share architectures, training families, datasets, and in one case a teacher. No uncertainty over either axis or robustness analysis excluding individual model families is provided.

The proposed object-centric metric is essentially ROC-AUC of cosine affinity against COCO masks, and therefore is neither clearly novel nor free of object-level supervision as implied: ground-truth masks are required to compute it. Details such as treatment of partial/boundary patches, multiple overlapping annotations, background, object-size weighting, and repeated central-object measurements are insufficiently specified.

Noise-ceiling normalization is not fully justified. The split-half correlation of 0.42 is used directly without a Spearman-Brown correction or a derivation of the appropriate ceiling for predictions evaluated against the group mean. The resulting normalized values, such as 0.83 for DINOv3, should not be interpreted as fractions of attainable human-level performance without this clarification. Statistical uncertainty and paired comparisons between models are also missing.

The participant population is narrow, and the benchmark uses only COCO scenes selected to satisfy particular overlap and dot-placement constraints. The paper does not quantify selection bias or demonstrate generalization to other datasets, object configurations, or participant populations. Code and data are said to be available 'here,' but no usable anonymized link or release details appear in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.

The manuscript is generally clear and its figures communicate the experimental design and principal results effectively. The comparison covers multiple self-supervised objectives, supervised ViTs, and ConvNeXt models. The results consistently suggest that DINO-family dense features contain more object-boundary information than the selected supervised counterparts.

Several useful robustness checks are included: a linear readout preserves the model ranking, condition-wise model-human correlations are reported, raw correlations accompany normalized values, and CLS-token distillation is tested as a control for Gram alignment.

The authors appropriately report accuracy, d-prime, response criterion, fixation-break exclusions, and ethics approval. The raw behavioral data appear reliable, with high task accuracy and above-chance RT structure.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is better assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks or Concept & Feasibility contribution than as a new algorithm. Under that framing, the behavioral dataset and model-comparison question are more significant than the technically simple metric and readouts.
weaknesses: The principal RT-prediction evaluation appears to have serious image leakage. The 1,020 trials consist of four dot conditions for each of 255 underlying images, yet the stated 10-fold cross-validation splits trials rather than grouping all four variants of an image. Consequently, test images will generally have three closely related variants in training, including the identical central-patch representation. The highly overparameterized two-layer MLP can therefore learn image-specific difficulty from roughly 918 training trials. Averaging seeds and nested early stopping do not fix this dependence. Grouped-by-image cross-validation is essential, and its absence undermines the main behavioral-alignment rankings and the Gram-alignment conclusions derived from them.

The experiments do not establish that the models capture specifically human-like grouping rather than easier task and stimulus correlates. Mean RT is strongly separated by same/different condition, while the readout is trained directly on RT. Missing baselines include predictors using only response category, dot distance, mask geometry or boundary distance, central/peripheral location, and low-level image statistics. Within-condition correlations help but remain modest (0.32–0.43 for the best model) and are still subject to the image-leakage problem.

The noise-ceiling normalization is not justified and likely inflates the headline values. A split-half correlation of 0.42 is divided directly into model-human correlations, producing 0.83 from a raw correlation of 0.348. Split-half reliability normally requires correction for the full participant set and a carefully defined ceiling; correlations normalized for measurement reliability are not generally obtained by simply dividing by the uncorrected split-half correlation. The raw correlations are much more modest and should be primary unless the normalization is formally justified.

The claimed link between object-centricity and behavioral alignment rests on only nine non-independent models (Spearman r=0.95). Architecture, objective, pretraining data, generation, distillation, and training scale are confounded rather than factorially controlled. DINOv3 models also occupy the high end of both axes, making the correlation vulnerable to family and scale effects. This evidence supports an association within this selected model set, not the asserted general principle or the conclusion that training objective contributes more strongly than architecture.

The Gram experiment does not isolate Gram structure as a causal mechanism. Matching the complete pairwise token-similarity matrix of the best DINOv3 teacher directly transfers precisely the representation property used by the object-centric AUC, so improvement in that metric is close to expected by construction. CLS distillation is a weak control because it transfers no dense token-level information. Necessary controls include token-feature distillation, alternative relational losses, shuffled or spatially disrupted Gram targets, different teachers, matched fine-tuning baselines, and independent images/tasks. No uncertainty estimates or statistical tests over training runs are shown for Figure 7.

The proposed object-centric metric is essentially ROC-AUC evaluation of whether patch similarity retrieves pixels within a ground-truth segmentation mask, closely related to established dense-feature and unsupervised-segmentation evaluations. It also requires COCO object masks at evaluation time, contrary to the potentially misleading contribution wording that it measures boundaries 'without requiring object-level supervision.' Its novelty and distinction from prior affinity-based segmentation metrics need much stronger positioning.

Behavioral analysis is incomplete for the strength of the perceptual claims. The paper does not report mixed-effects or repeated-measures tests for the same-object and distance interaction, RT trimming and transformation rules, anticipatory/slow-response handling, or uncertainty over trial-level model correlations. Excluding incorrect responses can also condition RT distributions. The sample is limited to undergraduate participants, which constrains claims about human perception.

Reproducibility details remain insufficient despite the stated code/data availability: the manuscript says only 'available here' without a usable link, leaves readout hyperparameter-selection ranges unspecified, and does not clearly document all preprocessing, patch-to-dot assignment, Gram-training duration, random-seed variability, or confidence intervals. Overall, the benchmark is promising, but consequential evaluation leakage and unsupported causal/mechanistic claims prevent a convincing case for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question at the intersection of computer vision and human perception, and its combination of psychophysics, representation analysis, and model intervention is more informative than a benchmark comparison alone.

The behavioral benchmark is substantial and carefully designed: 72 participants, 255 natural images, four distance/object conditions, counterbalancing, eye tracking, and fixation-based trial exclusion. Accuracy, d-prime, response bias, and condition-specific reaction-time analyses support the reliability of the measurements.

The empirical pattern is coherent across several analyses. DINO-family representations yield better grouping accuracy and reaction-time prediction, object-centric AUC increases across DINOv3 layers, and the best model predicts variation within every experimental condition rather than merely reproducing condition means.

The model set usefully spans supervised and self-supervised training, Transformer and convolutional architectures, and multiple model generations. The MAE and distilled ConvNext results provide informative intermediate cases.

The proposed affinity-based object-centricity measure is simple, interpretable, and strongly associated with behavioral alignment across the nine tested models. The Gram-alignment experiment and CLS-token control provide suggestive evidence that patch-similarity structure is functionally relevant.

The supplementary linear-readout result, raw correlations, condition-wise correlations, and classification-performance checks address several plausible alternative explanations. The manuscript is generally clear and its figures communicate the main results effectively.
weaknesses: The most important methodological concern is that the 10-fold reaction-time evaluation appears to split the 1,020 trials randomly rather than grouping folds by image. Each of the 255 images contributes four trials with an identical central patch and related scene features, so conditions from a test image will usually occur in training. This can inflate generalization by allowing image-specific information to cross folds. A leave-images-out evaluation is necessary; participant-wise or independent-image replication would further strengthen the behavioral claim.

The noise-ceiling normalization is not well justified. The paper divides model-to-half-subject correlation by the split-half correlation (0.42), although these quantities do not generally share the same attainable upper bound; reliability correction commonly requires Spearman-Brown adjustment and/or a square-root correction. Thus normalized values such as 0.83 may substantially overstate proximity to the human ceiling, even if raw correlations and model rankings remain informative.

Claims that training objective is the key causal factor are stronger than the comparisons permit. Model generations differ in data scale, training recipes, registers, and other details, while DINOv3 ConvNext is distilled from a Transformer. The manuscript acknowledges incomplete decoupling in one place but repeatedly makes stronger objective-versus-architecture conclusions elsewhere.

The Gram experiment supports transfer from a strong teacher but does not yet isolate Gram structure convincingly. Figure 7 compares Gram-aligned models with the original bases, rather than reporting grouping, AUC, and behavioral results for identically fine-tuned no-Gram controls. The CLS control covers only two ViTs and does not rule out benefits from generic dense-feature distillation. Exact results, uncertainty across training runs, and matched controls should be reported before describing Gram structure as a mechanism that drives alignment.

The reported correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment uses only nine highly related, non-independent model variants. Both measures are also evaluated on the same restricted COCO image set, and both may co-vary with overall representation quality. The impressive Spearman correlation is therefore descriptive rather than strong evidence for a general principle; broader model families and independent images are needed.

The benchmark is restricted to COCO scenes selected to contain overlapping annotated objects with one object at the image center. COCO instance masks, patch discretization, and manual exclusions may also privilege conventional semantic object boundaries. Generalization to non-COCO imagery, unannotated background regions, ambiguous boundaries, and other forms of perceptual grouping is not established.

Reproducibility information remains incomplete: the manuscript says code and data are available “here,” but the supplied PDF contains no usable link. Gram-alignment training duration, augmentation and preprocessing details, checkpoint selection, statistical uncertainty, and exact numerical values for several central plots are also insufficiently reported.

No contribution type is declared, so I assessed it under Algorithms/General as instructed. Its strongest contribution is arguably a behavioral benchmark and empirical analysis rather than a new algorithm; viewed as Datasets/Benchmarks work, release accessibility, documentation, licensing, and independent validation become especially important and are not yet demonstrated in the manuscript.
